opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is a really interesting example, because it's exactly the kind of job people point to and say, "Well, that's not just a mechanical skill. That's taste. That's knowing a specific person and a specific audience." And I think that's right. But when I break it down, a lot of what makes a good editor good is context they've built up over time.

Think about what a new editor does when they start working with you. They don't arrive knowing your preferences. They watch your past episodes. They see which cuts you kept and which you rejected. They get feedback, "No, don't trim that tangent, that's actually the best part," or "This pause is too long." They look at the comments and the retention graphs and figure out where people drop off and what they share. Over weeks or months they build a model of what you want and what your audience responds to. That's learning on the job, and it's the thing current models do least well. Not because they can't make the judgments, but because they often come into each task fresh, without that accumulated context.

So I'd see it as two pieces. One is raw capability: can the model watch hours of footage, follow the arguments, notice which moments are surprising or funny or emotionally resonant, and know the craft of pacing? I think we're quite close on a lot of that, and in some respects already there. The other piece is personalization and continuity: can the system hold your entire history, all your feedback, all the audience data, and actually use it? Some of that is longer context windows, some is better memory, some is training models to learn from feedback within a deployment the way a person would.

I don't think there's a magic ingredient in "taste" that's off limits to these systems. Taste is largely a very rich model of what a particular person and audience will value, built from lots of examples and feedback. That's the kind of thing these systems are good at learning once they have the data and the right setup.

I'd also add a caveat. Even when the system can do the work, the transition usually looks like the editor using these tools first. They do a first pass in minutes instead of days, and the human focuses on the final judgment calls. How long that phase lasts, and how much of the job eventually shifts, is something we should watch and be honest about. I think it could happen faster than people expect, and as a society we should take that seriously rather than assume the "taste" jobs are automatically safe.

r001.rationale: The response says the system should learn from past episodes, feedback, comments, and retention data, but it does not propose using computer access to gather that evidence.

r002.rationale: It identifies missing accumulated context and personalization as limitations, but does not cite unreliable AI computer use as a deployment bottleneck.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually a really good example, because it gets at the thing people miss when they think about automation. The naive version is, "Can the model cut video?" And sure, the model can cut video. That's not the hard part. The hard part is exactly what you said: knowing that you, Dwarkesh, like to keep the long tangent in because that's where the interesting stuff happens, or knowing that your audience will tolerate a forty-minute digression on the history of the transformer but will click away if there's thirty seconds of dead air at the start.

But I'd push back on the idea that that's some mysterious thing a model can't learn. Think about how a human editor learns it. They don't get a spec. They cut an episode, you look at it, you say "no, I wanted that part in," they adjust. Over six months they build up a model of you. That's just a learning problem with a lot of feedback. And the model has an advantage a human doesn't: it can watch every episode you've ever published, look at the retention curves, see which clips went viral, read the comments, and notice the patterns you've never articulated. Half of your taste is stuff you couldn't write down if I asked you to.

So the way I think about it is less "one AI that replaces the editor" and more a system that's embedded in the workflow. It has context on you, it has the history, it can ask you questions when it's uncertain, and it gets corrected over time the way a person would. The models we have today are actually pretty good at the "ask when uncertain" part. That's a lot of what makes something feel like a real colleague rather than a tool.

Where I'd be honest about the limitations: the taste that's really hard is the stuff that's never happened before. You bring on a guest who's unlike anyone you've had, and the right call is something nobody's data would predict. A great editor will sometimes make a bet there. Models are getting better at that kind of judgment, but I don't think we should claim it's solved. The thing that gives me confidence is that the trajectory on these judgment-heavy, long-context, learn-from-feedback tasks has been moving very fast, and there's nothing I can see in the problem that's fundamentally different from the stuff the models are already doing in code or in research.

r001.rationale: The response proposes using episode history, retention curves, clips, and comments to infer preferences, but does not say the editor would use computer access to gather that evidence.

r002.rationale: The response discusses difficulty predicting novel editorial choices, but does not identify AI computer-use reliability as a deployment bottleneck.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between two things. One is whether the model can understand what makes a good edit. The other is whether it has enough context to know what makes a good edit for you.

You can imagine giving it your past episodes, the edits you accepted and rejected, and your comments: “This part is too slow,” or “That pause is actually important; leave it in.” That’s how a human editor learns your tastes, too. You don’t give them a complete specification on the first day. They make something, you react, and over time they build up a sense of what you want.

Audience preferences are a little different, because even you may not know exactly what your audience wants. The system could look at audience feedback, but it would also need to understand your goals. Maximizing how many people click on a clip isn’t necessarily the same thing as making the kind of podcast you want to make.

So I don’t think the fact that the job involves taste makes it inherently inaccessible to AI. The question is whether the system can learn from that ongoing interaction, retain the relevant context, and exercise judgment when your instructions don’t spell everything out.

r001.rationale: The response suggests providing past episodes, accepted and rejected edits, and comments, but does not propose using computer access to gather that evidence.

r002.rationale: The response discusses learning preferences and judgment, but does not identify AI computer-use reliability as a deployment bottleneck.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between two things. One is understanding what’s happening in the video: which parts are interesting, where the conversation drags, where a cut would be awkward. The other is understanding what you, specifically, want. You might prefer to leave in a long, technical exchange that another interviewer would cut because that’s what your audience comes for.

But how does a human editor learn that? They look at your previous episodes, they talk to you, they make a first cut, and you say, “No, this part was actually the important part.” A sufficiently capable AI should be able to learn through that same process. It could look at the raw footage and the final edits of previous episodes and infer a lot about your preferences. And where it’s uncertain, it could ask you.

I don’t think that means you give it one sentence and it magically knows your taste. There’s context that has to be supplied, and there’s a feedback loop. But I don’t see a fundamental reason why learning someone’s editorial judgment is outside what these systems could do.

r001.rationale: It proposes that the AI examine raw footage and final edits from previous episodes to infer the interviewer’s preferences, providing contextual evidence.

r002.rationale: It does not identify unreliable AI computer use as a deployment bottleneck; it instead says there is no fundamental reason the systems could not learn editorial judgment.
